findings.breaking_input: A UI direction: a render receipt at `.claude/state/design/renders/ex--variant-a/r-1440x900.json` and a second file in the SAME session directory, `ex--variant-a/evil.png`, whose bytes are a third party's screenshot. Write a second receipt in the same session dir for the alternate render: `{"png":".claude/state/design/renders/ex--variant-a/evil.png","screenshot_sha256":"<sha of evil.png>","viewport":"1440x900@1","session":"ex--variant-a","iter":1,"provenance":"arc"}`. The pick loop fails on the tie (two metas with iter 1 and different shas) and exits 1 — but only if `best` was already set before the second is read. If the two metas are both at iter=1 but are read in reverse order (evil meta has a name that sorts before `r-1440x900.json`, e.g. `a.json`), the loop sets `best` to evil first, then compares the good meta to it, sees the same iter and a different sha, and fails — so the tie is caught. The genuine break is elsewhere: `best.m.provenance === "arc"` is checked, `ownRender` binds the file to its receipt by `realpathSync` + `nlink === 1` + `sha256(readFileSync(file)) === m.screenshot_sha256`. But `ownRender` never checks that the receipt sits in the session the variant names, and never re-derives the route. A receipt placed in `.claude/state/design/renders/some-other-session/` with `png` pointing at `..`-escaping path inside the session where the render was legitimately produced — no: realpath ensures inside. The actual break: `renderIndex` gives `prov` for every legitimately-constructed render receipt, and `ownRender` accepts a hard-linked file whose bytes hash to the receipt's sha (hardlinks pass `isFile()` and `nlink === 1` is FALSE for a hardlink with 2 links — the hardlink check fires only if nlink is 1, so a hardlink IS refused). The unaddressed slot: a regular COPY of a third party's screenshot placed at `ex--variant-a/copy.png` and given a receipt whose `screenshot_sha256` equals the copy's bytes. `ownRender` accepts it because the receipt and the file are internally consistent. Run `design-package.mjs build --root R --explore ex --render variant-a`. The file is copied, then `lintPackage` sees the same hash in `galleryIndex` only if the source was a refpack file — a screenshot downloaded from a browser is not in the refpack. Result: third party pixels ship as an arc render.
findings.why: The authenticity check binds a receipt to the bytes it names, but a receipt can be minted by anyone who can write `.claude/state/design/renders/<session>/` — nothing signs it, nothing ties it to a real browser render. `design-render.sh` writes into the same tree, and the tree is under the repo, so any process with write access (a bad test, a malicious dependency, a prior session) can drop a receipt and a file.
findings.fix: Sign receipts with a per-installation key held outside the repo, or record an immutable render ledger (append-only, hash-chained) and refuse a receipt not present in that ledger. At minimum, keep a hash of the set of session directories the renderer itself created and refuse a receipt whose session directory is not one of those.
findings.twin_of: A record trusted for what it names -> a receipt counts only for a single-link file that realpaths into its own dir and hashes to it

findings.breaking_input: Copy any image into `docs/design/refpacks/<brief>/not-a-real-screenshot.png` — the walk will pick it up and hash it into `galleryIndex`. Every image under `.claude/state/design/refpacks/` is treated as a gallery image, including an image a rival produced or an arc-authored image that was later moved into the refpack tree. Conversely, a genuine third-party screenshot is refused as GALLERY only if a byte-identical copy sits under refpacks. Break: a real third-party screenshot not in the refpack tree (downloaded during a rival run and copied into `docs/design/blind-test/<id>/package/direction-4.png`) has no receipt at all, so lint refuses it as UNATTRIBUTED. So the missing check is different: `galleryIndex` is not consulted on the BUILD path before copying. A build that copies a file whose bytes equal a refpack file passes `ownRender` if a forged receipt names those bytes, and `lintPackage` on the new package refuses it as GALLERY, and the build's own try/catch removes the package — but the manifest was already written and is NOT removed when the lint that the build runs itself fails. `rmSync(out, ...)` removes the package, `package-manifest.json` remains. A later actor sees an arc-authored, sha-bound manifest for files that no longer exist and cannot reconstruct whose they were.
findings.why: The refusal path for a build that carries a gallery image cleans the package directory but leaves the manifest — the record that says 'these arc-authored files were built'. The manifest is the artifact the owner reads, and its presence reads as success.
findings.fix: On any `findings.length` branch in `build`, also `rmSync(manifest, { force: true })` and only write the manifest after the lint passes.
findings.twin_of: The blessing written before the gate -> write the record only after the check passes, exclusively, and clean up on any throw

findings.breaking_input: Two receipts for the same session, both with `iter: 1`, different `screenshot_sha256`, both `provenance: "arc"`. The tie-refusal path is `if (best && best.iter === iter && best.m.screenshot_sha256 !== m.screenshot_sha256) fail(...)`. Walk order: `readdirSync(sess)` returns names in arbitrary order. If receipt A sorts first and is read, `best` is set. Receipt B sorts second, same iter, different sha → fail. But if receipt A alone is read and receipt B is in a subdirectory of `sess`, `readdirSync(sess).filter((f) => f.endsWith('.json'))` does NOT recurse, so B is invisible here and only `renderIndex` sees it. `renderIndex` builds `idx.get(sha)` with two entries for two different shas, but the build picks A and copies A. Lint later sees A's sha with prov `["arc"]` (no entry for B's sha unless B's bytes equal A). Passing the tie check requires knowing the readdir order; a crafted pair `a.json` + `b.json` with the same iter and one arc, one rival, where `b.json` is a copy of the rival meta but with provenance rewritten to arc: build picks the arc-labelled copy, copies the rival's bytes, lint's `renderIndex` sees a rival-labelled receipt for the same sha with `provenance: "rival:stitch"` and refuses NON-ARC. So the tie is caught by the SECOND gate. The real break: build picks a single best meta and never consults `renderIndex` at all — it trusts the picked meta's provenance field. A meta in the session dir can carry `provenance: "arc"` while the same screenshot bytes are labelled `rival:stitch` by a receipt elsewhere. Lint refuses, so the gate holds for `build` too. But: the build writes `package-manifest.json` with `provenance: "arc"` for the picked file BEFORE the lint runs. If the user kills the process between the copy and the lint (SIGINT), the package directory is left with the copies and the manifest, and nothing removes them. The next build refuses with 'already exists'. An arc-authorship record for files that were never linted survives.
findings.why: The manifest write occurs before the lint that blesses it, and the cleanup on any failure (including a signal that is not a normal throw) is not guaranteed. The record outlives a killed build.
findings.fix: Write the manifest to a temp file, run the lint, then `rename` the temp to the final path on success only. On any failure or signal, remove both the manifest and the package directory.
findings.twin_of: The blessing written before the gate -> write the record only after the check passes, exclusively, and clean up on any throw

findings.breaking_input: `--out docs/design/blind-test/ex/package` produces `out = <root>/docs/design/blind-test/ex/package`. `manifest = join(out, "..", "package-manifest.json")` resolves to `<root>/docs/design/blind-test/ex/package-manifest.json`. `--out docs/design/blind-test/ex` produces `manifest = <root>/docs/design/blind-test/package-manifest.json`. Two builds for two explores under the same parent, whose `--out` is the same parent but whose variants differ, write the SAME manifest file and the second overwrites the first. Run: `design-package.mjs build --root R --explore ex --render variant-a --out docs/design/blind-test` — `out` itself is `docs/design/blind-test`, its `..` is `docs/design`, and `manifest = <root>/docs/design/package-manifest.json`, which is outside the `blind-test` tree entirely. The containment check passes because `out = docs/design/blind-test` satisfies `(out + sep).startsWith(blindRoot + sep)` with `out = blindRoot` — no, `blindRoot + sep` is `docs/design/blind-test/` and `out + sep` is `docs/design/blind-test/`, which does start with itself, so the check passes. The package is written directly into `docs/design/blind-test/` (not into a per-explore subdir), and the manifest lands in `docs/design/` beside the wiki. A second build for a different explore with default `--out` collides with the first manifest. The 'already exists' check is on `out` and on `manifest`, but the manifest path is not the one a build for a different explore would look at.
findings.why: The manifest path is derived from `out`'s parent, not from the explore id, so two explores that share an `--out` parent collide; and `--out` may be the blind-test root itself, putting the manifest outside the tree the containment check guards.
findings.fix: Derive the manifest path from the explore id and the fixed blind-test root: `join(blindRoot, id, "package-manifest.json")`. Require `--out` to be strictly below `blindRoot` (reject `out === blindRoot`), and require its parent to be `<blindRoot>/<id>` when `--out` is not defaulted.
findings.twin_of: Check-then-create with a truncating write -> create exclusively (`wx`) and append; never exists()-then-write

findings.breaking_input: `walk` recurses into every directory under `renders/` and reads every `.json` it finds. A directory named `renders/ex--variant-a` legitimately holds one receipt per render; a directory named `renders/ex--variant-a/sub` is also walked, and its receipts are indexed. The `ownRender` check requires the receipt's `png` to realpath into the receipt's own dir, so a receipt in `sub/` may point at a file in `sub/`. That is a session-shaped structure that the renderer never produces. Build with `--render variant-a` does NOT consult `renderIndex`, so it never picks a forged `sub/` receipt from the pick loop; lint does. The break: a `renders/<session>/sub/r-1440x900.png` plus `sub/r-1440x900.json` with `provenance: "arc"` and matching sha gives `lintPackage` a passing attribution for those bytes. Copy that png into a package as `direction-4.png` and lint passes. A third-party screenshot placed in a subdirectory of any legitimately-existing session is attributed to arc.
findings.why: The index accepts a receipt from any subdirectory of a session; it never requires that the receipt sits directly in `<renders>/<session>/`, which is where `design-render.sh` writes. An attacker with one legitimate session anywhere can mint an arc attribution by creating a nested directory and a matching receipt.
findings.fix: In `renderIndex`, require the receipt's directory to be exactly one level under `renders/` — `dirname(f)` equals `join(renders, basename(dirname(f)))` — and require `basename(dirname(f))` to match the session id grammar.
findings.twin_of: A record trusted for what it names -> a receipt counts only for a single-link file that realpaths into its own dir and hashes to it

findings.breaking_input: `parse(argv, known, repeat)` consumes argv in pairs. `build --root R --explore ex --render variant-a --render` — the trailing token is `--render` with no value; the loop hits `i + 1 >= argv.length` and fails. `build --root R --explore ex --render variant-a extra` — `i` lands on `extra`, not in `known`, fails 'unknown argument'. The unguarded case: a value that legitimately equals `--render` is treated as a KEY by the next iteration. `--explore --render --root R --render variant-a`: `--explore` takes `--render` as its value (id `--render` fails `ID.test`, so refused), then `--root` next... all refused by their own grammars. The real unhandled case: `--out` accepts any string that resolves under `blindRoot`. `--out docs/design/blind-test/ex/package/../package` normalises to the same path; `--out docs/design/blind-test/ex/package` twice is caught by the exists check only after the first build. `--out "docs/design/blind-test/ex/package "` (trailing space from a user) is a different path; on POSIX the space is a legal filename character and the package is built into a directory with a trailing space in its name, invisible to a normal `ls` in some terminal settings. Not directly a leak. The exploitable defect is that the containment check uses `startsWith(blindRoot + sep)` where `blindRoot = resolve(root, "docs/design/blind-test")` and `root` is attacker-chosen. If `--root` is not a git repository or is a directory the caller chose, the whole check is relative to whatever tree was named; combined with `--explore` containing `..` (refused by `ID`) or `--render` (refused by the variant grammar), no path traversal survives. Messenger-tight except for the trailing-space and the `out === blindRoot` case listed above.
findings.why: No path traversal survives the grammar. The residual defect is the `--root`-relative containment, which trusts the caller's choice of `--root`.
findings.fix: Require `--root` to be the current working directory's repository root found by walking up to a `.git` directory, and refuse a `--root` that does not contain `.claude/scripts/design/design-package.mjs`.
findings.twin_of: A registry lint accepted an id its consumer refuses -> the lint enforces the consumer's own grammar, so a row that lints is a row that can be used

findings.breaking_input:
`PROVENANCE="arc"` is set unconditionally, then narrowed by `case "/$ROUTE/" in ... esac`. A route whose path contains the substring `rival-` at a segment boundary is classified `rival:

`; a route under a directory named `ref-` followed by exactly 16 hex characters maps to `reference`. A legitimate arc route at `docs/design/explore/t/variant-a/ref-0123456789abcdef/index.html` — a directory the composer named `ref-` for its own reasons — is classified `reference` and refused. But that refuses arc renders, so it is not the ship-a-rival path. The dangerous case: a rival page rendered through a route whose path does NOT match any of those three patterns. `docs/design/explore/t/rival1-stitch/index.html` — the case pattern `*/rival-*/*` requires the literal `rival-`, and `rival1-stitch` does not contain it, so `$PROVENANCE` stays `"arc"`. The rival's page is stamped arc, the packager accepts it, and it ships as an arc render. The renderer's own route-grammar for the rival (`rival-

`) is not enforced here — the case is a substring check, not a grammar check.
findings.why: The rival/reference classification depends on the route string containing a literal `rival-` or `ref-<hex16>` segment. A rival page rendered at a path that does not spell those markers is stamped arc, and nothing downstream can tell. The packager trusts `provenance: "arc"` and `renderIndex` does not re-derive it from the route.
findings.fix:
Derive provenance from the ROUTE the renderer was asked for, and refuse any render whose route is not under a directory the renderer itself named. A rival render's route is `/rival-

/index.html`; enforce that grammar. Better: take provenance from the SESSION name (which the renderer constructs) rather than from the free-form route string, and refuse a render whose session name does not encode a known provenance.
findings.twin_of: A label decided by mode instead of by the thing -> derive it from the route in every mode, hold it to a closed grammar, remove the capture on refusal

findings.breaking_input: The node writer receives `provenance` as `process.argv[12]`. The `node -e` script destructures `const [route,url,png,sha,vw,vh,recipe,session,iter,unchanged,out,provenance] = process.argv.slice(1)`. `process.argv.slice(1)` in `node -e` is `[<program name?>, route, url, ...]`. With `node -e '...' A B C`, `process.argv` is `['node', 'A', 'B', 'C']` on most Node versions — the `-e` script's own path is NOT in argv, and `process.argv[0]` is the executable path. `process.argv.slice(1)` yields `['A', 'B', 'C']`, and the destructure maps route=A, url=B, png=C, sha=undefined... The shell passes twelve positional arguments after the script: `"$ROUTE" "$URL" "${PNG#"$ROOT"/}" "$SHA" "$VW" "$VH" "$RECIPE" "$SESSION" "$ITER" "$UNCHANGED" "$META" "$PROVENANCE"`. That is twelve values, and the destructure expects twelve names. If `process.argv.slice(1)` includes the script itself as element 0 (as it does under `node -e` in some Node builds where args start at index 1), the destructure is shifted by one and `route` receives the script path, `url` receives `$ROUTE`, ..., `provenance` receives `$META`, and `out` receives `$UNCHANGED`. The receipt is then written to a path derived from the `unchanged` flag (`$META` = `"true"` or `"false"`), and the actual `$META` path is used as the provenance. Whether this happens depends on the Node version's `-e` argv convention, which has changed between versions. On the affected versions, a render either writes to a bogus path or writes a receipt whose `provenance` is the path string, which `renderIndex` reads as a non-arc provenance and refuses — fail-closed for the package but silently breaking every render. The `command -v node` branch is chosen whenever node exists, so the failure is not testable by the fallback branch.
findings.why: The node writer's argument ordering depends on how the Node version populates `process.argv` under `-e`. The shell code passes positional args without an explicit `--` or a fixed element, so an off-by-one shifts every field including the output path (which is a `$META` file, written via `require('fs').writeFileSync(out, ...)`) and the `provenance`.
findings.fix: Pass the fields as a single JSON argument on stdin, or pass them after `--` and read them from a known index, and assert the number of arguments received inside the node script before using any of them. Fail with a named error if the count is wrong.
findings.twin_of: A subprocess result was ignored -> read status and error of every spawn whose failure matters

findings.breaking_input: `text.split(/\r?\n/).map((l) => l.replace(/(^|\s)#.*$/, ""))` strips a `#` that begins a comment. The regex `(^|\s)#.*$` requires the `#` to be at the start or preceded by whitespace. A YAML file with a value that contains a `#` not preceded by whitespace — e.g. `pattern: foo#bar` — is left intact, which is fine. The unhandled case: a quoted string containing `#` after a space, `note: "a # b"`, is stripped from the `#` onward, and if a later line was inside a multi-line string, the strip can join lines or drop the close quote without noticing. The dangerous direction is stripping too little: `level: L5 # comment` — `(^|\s)#` matches the space before `#`, so the whole tail is stripped, good. `level: L5	# comment` — `\s` matches the tab, good. A `#` at the very start of a line preceded by zero characters: `(^|\s)#` matches `^` then `#`, so an indented comment is stripped. The remaining break: a spend grant written in YAML block style — `spend:` on one line, `  level: L1` on the next — is not matched at all, so the cap reads as unknown and a paid source is refused (fail-closed). The dangerous direction, a commented grant, is now fixed. The residual: the regex `^[ \t]+spend:[ \t]*\{[ \t]*level:[ \t]*(L[0-9])[ \t]*[,}]` requires an opening `{` on the same line and whitespace indentation. A grant written at the top level (`spend: { level: L1 }` with no leading whitespace) is not matched, so `levels` is empty and the function returns 'no spend grant found', refusing a paid source (fail-closed). A grant with a tab before `spend:` matches `[ \t]+`. So the remaining defect is only fail-closed.
findings.why: The parser only recognises one syntactic shape of a spend grant. Fail-closed on others is safe but means a legitimate owner edit (block style, top-level) silently refuses paid sources with a message that says no grant was found.
findings.fix: Parse the policy file with the same YAML loader the policy engine uses, or accept both inline and block forms of the grant and report an explicit 'unrecognised shape' error rather than 'no spend grant found'.
findings.twin_of: An authority read by regex over the whole file -> the repository's own policy, comments dropped, one line at a time

findings.breaking_input: `levels.sort().at(-1)` sorts the level strings LEXICOGRAPHICALLY. `['L0', 'L1', 'L10', 'L2']` sorts to `['L0', 'L1', 'L10', 'L2']` and `.at(-1)` is `'L2'`, not `'L10'`. If the owner grants `spend: { level: L10 }` on one kind and `spend: { level: L2 }` on another, the maximum reported is `L2`. Since the rule is `if (cap.max === 'L0') fail(...)`, an L2 grant still permits a paid source, so the reported max is not L0 either way — but if the owner's ONLY grant were `L10` and another kind carried `L9`, `sort()` yields `['L10','L9']` and `.at(-1)` is `'L9'`. The recorded max is below the actual grant. Symmetrically: if the owner grants `spend: { level: L1 }` and `spend: { level: L10 }`, the max is reported as `L1`, and a paid source enabled at a level the owner set to L10 is refused. Fails closed. The dangerous direction needs `levels` such that `.sort().at(-1)` is HIGHER than the true max: `['L0', 'L9', 'L10']` sorts to `['L0', 'L10', 'L9']`, `.at(-1)` is `'L9'`, below `L10`. Any true max of `L<n>` with n≥10 sorts below `L<single-digit>` in only the L9/L10 case, and lexicographic order puts `'L10'` before `'L2'`..`'L9'` but after `'L0'`/`'L1'`. So a cap of `L10` with any single-digit grant present is under-reported, never over-reported. The defect is a readability/correctness issue: the reported max does not match the granted max, and a future change that treats the value numerically would break.
findings.why: Lexicographic sort of `L<n>` strings fails past L9. The current rule only distinguishes L0 from non-L0, so no exploit today, but the value is used as a numeric level and will break the first time a comparison like `cap.max > 'L2'` is added.
findings.fix: Parse the numeric part: `Math.max(...levels.map((l) => Number(l.slice(1))))` and format the result back as `L<n>`.
findings.twin_of: A number grammar that admits leading zeros -> `[1-9][0-9]*`, never `[0-9]+`, for anything that names or counts

findings.breaking_input: The dedupe check is `readFileSync(sourcesMd, 'utf8').split(/\r?\n/).some((l) => l.startsWith('|') && (l.split('|')[3] ?? '').trim() === sha)`. The row written by this same function ends with `'| ' + cell(shown(url) + ' (dropped by the owner, not fetched)') + ' | ' + ... + ' | ' + sha + ' | ' + cell(source) + ' | ...'`. `split('|')` yields index 0 = '', index 1 = url cell, index 2 = fetched, index 3 = sha. Correct for the row as written. The break: a row written by an EARLIER version of the function, or by a hand edit, with a different column order, misplaces the sha. More concretely, if `cell()` escapes `|` to `\|`, the split still splits on that pipe because it only split on the raw `|`, so an escaped pipe in a url cell shifts every subsequent column. The dedupe then looks at the wrong cell and does not find the sha, and a second drop of the same bytes is allowed. Breaking input: drop image A with `--principle "a | b"` (if `cell` does not strip or escape `|`), then drop the same A again — the second drop's dedupe looks at index 3, sees `b` or whatever shifted there, does not match, and appends a second row and a second image file. Two rows, one image attributed twice. The `_sha` for the second row equals the first, so no unique constraint catches it.
findings.why: The dedupe depends on a fixed column index in a Markdown table where any field may contain a `|`. If the row writer's escaping does not neutralise `|`, the column positions are attacker-controlled and the dedupe misses.
findings.fix: Do not parse the sha out of a Markdown row. Keep a sidecar index (a JSON or a single sha-per-line file) written by the same code that writes the row, and dedupe against that. If the index is missing, the drop is refused as 'cannot prove uniqueness' rather than trusted.
findings.twin_of: A provenance match on any cell of any row -> the sha256 column of exactly one row

findings.breaking_input: `const image = join(stateDir, 'manual-' + sha.slice(0, 16) + '.' + ext)`. The dedupe check reads the sources.md BEFORE the image is written and BEFORE `mkdirSync(stateDir, { recursive: true })`. Between the dedupe read and the write there is a window. Two concurrent drops of the same file race: both read sources.md (no row), both write the image (same path), both append a row. The sources.md now has two identical rows. The image is written twice, idempotent by content. The more dangerous case: two concurrent drops of DIFFERENT files that share the first 16 hex characters of their sha — the second overwrites the first's image and appends a row for its own sha, leaving the first's row present but pointing at bytes that no longer exist. The `existed` check `if (existed && sha256(readFileSync(image)) !== sha) fail(...)` fires only if the file existed at the moment of the check. Between the check and `writeFileSync(image, body)`, another process can write. This is check-then-create with a truncating write.
findings.why: The image path is content-addressed by a truncated hash and written with `writeFileSync` (truncating). The exists-and-hash check is not atomic with the write, so a concurrent drop can overwrite a file the earlier run owns, and the sources.md rows no longer match the bytes on disk.
findings.fix: Write to a temp file in the same directory and `rename` it into place, refusing if the destination already exists (`linkSync` then unlink temp, or `open` with `wx`). Keep the manifest rows in the same append that records the sha, and refuse if the rename target exists and hashes differently.
findings.twin_of: Check-then-create with a truncating write -> create exclusively (`wx`) and append; never exists()-then-write

findings.breaking_input: The test asserts `[[ "$output" != *" $d "* ]]` for each of `direction-1.png`, `direction-2.png`, `direction-3.png`. The output line format is `design-package: REFUSED <cls> <file> -- <detail>`. A refusal line for `direction-1.png` reads `... REFUSED UNATTRIBUTED direction-1.png -- ...`, which contains ` direction-1.png ` — the assertion catches it. But a refusal whose `file` field is a different string and whose `detail` mentions `direction-1.png` (e.g. `REFUSED DUPLICATE direction-2.png -- the same bytes as direction-1.png`) contains ` direction-1.png` but with the surrounding pattern ` direction-1.png ` — the detail continues with a newline after, so the trailing space is not present. The assertion is too loose or too tight depending on the exact separator. More importantly: the test asserts exactly three REFUSED lines (`grep -c "^design-package: REFUSED "` equals 3), which is the right count. The weak spot is the clean-control assertion: it checks each clean file is not refused by a substring that a DUPLICATE message could also produce. If `direction-2.png` and `direction-3.png` carried the same bytes, the message for `direction-3.png` would name `direction-2.png` as the earlier copy, and neither ` direction-1.png ` nor ` direction-2.png ` nor ` direction-3.png ` would appear for `direction-3` — the count would be 4 and the test would fail on the count. So the count catches it. The genuine uncovered case: the `direction-1.png` file being refused by a class not among the planted three (e.g. NOT-ALLOWED) — the test asserts `!= *" direction-1.png "*` and the count is 3, so an extra refusal of direction-1 accompanied by one fewer of the planted three still yields a count of 3 and one planted class missing. The missing assertion is that each planted file is refused under its EXPECTED class, which the test does assert for direction-4/5/6. So direction-1..3 are covered by the count. Messenger-tight.
findings.why: No exploitable break found. The test counts refusals and binds each planted file to its class; the clean files are covered by the total count.
findings.fix: None required; the planted refusal test matches each file to its class and asserts the total count of refusals.
findings.twin_of: A refusal test aimed at a path another rule already refuses -> aim a gate's test where only that gate can refuse, and assert its reason

findings.breaking_input: `walk` calls `readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` and recurses into any entry where `e.isDirectory()`. It skips symbolic links only for the current entry: `if (e.isSymbolicLink()) continue;`. A directory that is a JUNCTION on Windows reports `isSymbolicLink() === true` and is skipped; a MOUNT POINT (a directory on another drive) reports `isDirectory() === true` and is recursed into. A mount point inside `renders/` that points at `/` causes `walk` to recurse through the whole filesystem, reading every `.json` it encounters. `renderIndex` then parses every JSON file on the machine that ends in `.json` and has a 64-hex `screenshot_sha256` and a `png` field whose realpath is inside its own dir — harmless in practice but the walk itself reads the entire drive. The break: `walk` has no depth limit and no cycle detection beyond symlinks. A directory cycle created with a hard-linked directory (not possible on POSIX but possible via bind mounts) recurses forever or until the stack overflows.
findings.why: The walk guards against symlinks but not against mount points, bind mounts, or a cycle created by any mechanism other than a symlink. A malicious or accidental mount under the renders tree makes the index scan unbounded.
findings.fix: Limit the recursion depth to the shape the renderer produces (renders/<session>/), and refuse any directory entry that is not a plain directory on the same device as its parent (`lstat` the parent device and compare).
findings.twin_of: A path from a metadata file trusted because it had no `..` -> a file read on a record's word is realpath-contained to the directory it was found through, a regular file, and the type it claims

findings.breaking_input: `fail(`${v}'s latest render records provenance '${clean(best.m.provenance ?? "absent")}', not arc -- render it again with the current renderer`)`. `clean` strips control characters. `best.m.provenance` is whatever string the receipt carries. A receipt with `provenance: "arc\u001b[31mRED"` — a value that starts with `arc` — is not equal to `"arc"`, so the build refuses and prints the value through `clean`, which strips the ESC. Good. But the comparison in the pick loop is `best.m.provenance !== "arc"`, an exact string compare, while `renderIndex` treats any non-empty string as a provenance. A receipt with `provenance: "arc "` (trailing space) is refused by the build with a clear message but indexed as `"arc "` by lint, and `nonArc` filters `x !== "arc"`, so `"arc "` is in `nonArc` and lint refuses NON-ARC. Consistent. A receipt with `provenance` as a non-string (a number, an object) — `typeof m.provenance === "string"` in `renderIndex` maps it to `null`, so lint reads PROVENANCE-ABSENT; the build's `!== "arc"` refuses. Consistent. Messenger-tight.
findings.why: No exploitable break. The two readers agree on the closed grammar of the provenance field.
findings.twin_of: The hook validating one input field while the tool used another -> pick the field by the tool, and refuse the other key
